title: YOU KEEP POSTING ABOUT JESUS… BUT WHEN WAS THE LAST TIME YOU ACTUALLY SAT ALONE WITH HIM?
paragraphs: YOU KEEP POSTING ABOUT JESUS… BUT WHEN WAS THE LAST TIME YOU ACTUALLY SAT ALONE WITH HIM?

Your timeline is full of Scripture. Your stories are full of worship. Your captions tell everyone how much you love God. But there's a question your followers cannot answer—and perhaps you've been afraid to answer it yourself: Does Jesus still have your attention when nobody is watching?
You posted about Jesus this morning.
Maybe it was a Bible verse. Maybe a worship song. Maybe a powerful reminder that God is faithful, that prayer changes things, that Jesus is coming again.
People reacted. Someone commented, “Amen.” Another person shared your post. Perhaps someone even messaged you to say your words were exactly what they needed.
And that matters. Don't misunderstand me.
God can use a simple post to reach a heart you may never meet.
But something happened after you put your phone down.
Or perhaps something didn't happen.

You had time to check who liked your post. Time to see who viewed your story. Time to scroll through someone else's life. Time to answer messages, watch videos, read comments, and return to your notifications more times than you can remember.
But somewhere in the middle of all that activity, there was Someone you never stopped to talk to.
The very Jesus you spent the morning telling everyone about.
And here is the question that might make you uncomfortable enough to keep reading:
What if you've become so busy talking about Jesus that you've slowly stopped talking to Jesus?
Not because you stopped believing.
Not because you deliberately walked away.
But because somewhere along the way, your public expression of faith became more consistent than your private communion with the One who saved you.
And the frightening part?
You can go a long time without noticing the difference.
Because religious activity can make spiritual distance look like spiritual maturity.
You can know how to encourage people while secretly feeling empty.
You can post about peace while your own heart is restless.
You can tell strangers to trust God while quietly carrying burdens you haven't brought before Him.
You can write about prayer without remembering the last time you prayed without rushing.
And you can become very good at describing a relationship that you've stopped intentionally nurturing.
That is not an accusation against every Christian who posts online.
It is an invitation to examine something only God and your own heart can truly see.
And before you assume this message is for somebody else, consider one more question.
If your phone stopped working tonight, would your relationship with Jesus still feel alive tomorrow morning?
Because there is a difference between having Christian content around you and having communion with Christ within your daily life.
One can fill your screen.
Only the other draws you into the presence of the living God.
And Jesus once walked into a home where that difference became painfully clear.
Martha was busy.
Not busy doing something sinful. Not wasting her time on meaningless distractions. She was serving. Preparing. Making sure things were ready.
And Jesus was in her house.
Imagine that.
The Son of God was physically present, and Martha was working hard to honor Him.
Meanwhile, her sister Mary sat at His feet, listening.
Eventually, Martha became frustrated.
She asked Jesus to tell Mary to help her.
And His response remains one of the most tender and confronting moments in Scripture.
“Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.” — Luke 10:41–42, KJV
In the Greek text, Luke describes Martha as περιεσπᾶτο (periespato) in verse 40, a word conveying the idea of being distracted or pulled away by her many preparations.
Then Jesus speaks of the ἀγαθὴν μερίδα (agathēn merida)—the good portion Mary had chosen.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say serving was worthless.
He did not say hospitality was sinful.
He did not condemn Martha for caring about practical responsibilities.
He lovingly corrected a situation in which many concerns had distracted her from what mattered most at that moment: receiving His words.
Martha was serving Jesus.
Mary was listening to Jesus.
And in that moment, Martha needed to remember that being occupied with things for the Lord must never replace attentiveness to the Lord Himself.
Now bring that story into our world.
Your kitchen may not be filled with preparations for an honored guest.
But your phone is filled with notifications.
Your schedule is filled with responsibilities.
Your mind is filled with unfinished conversations, financial worries, family concerns, deadlines, disappointments, and things you cannot control.
And perhaps your social media is filled with Jesus.
Yet your soul is starving for the quiet attention you haven't given Him.
You can be Martha with a smartphone.
Busy defending the faith. Busy posting Scripture. Busy encouraging others. Busy answering questions. Busy maintaining a Christian presence online.
All while the most important relationship in your life receives whatever attention is left over.
And sometimes there is nothing left.
But here is what makes this so personal.
You didn't necessarily intend for it to happen.
You remember when prayer felt different.
When you opened your Bible because you wanted to know God, not because you needed a caption.
When a passage of Scripture confronted you so deeply that you had to stop reading.
When you could sit quietly before the Lord without needing music playing, a camera recording, or someone else knowing what you were doing.
When repentance was more important than appearing spiritually strong.
When worship wasn't something you performed.
It was the response of a heart overwhelmed by grace.
Maybe you remember those days.
Maybe you miss them more than you admit.
Or maybe you have never experienced that kind of personal devotion and have quietly wondered whether your faith is supposed to be more than what you've known.
Either way, this invitation is for you.
Because Jesus did not save you merely to turn you into someone who produces religious content.
He saved you to reconcile you to God.
The apostle Peter describes Christ's suffering with these words:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God…” — 1 Peter 3:18, KJV
Read that final phrase again.
That He might bring us to God.
Not merely to a religious identity.
Not merely to a collection of Christian habits.
Not merely to a platform where we can speak about Him.
To God.
Through His death and resurrection, Jesus opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to the Father.
And sometimes we become so absorbed in the visible activities surrounding Christianity that we neglect the very fellowship with God that Christ died to make possible.
That should stop us in our tracks.
Because the cross was not a marketing strategy.
The empty tomb was not a content opportunity.
The blood of Jesus was not shed so that we could look spiritually impressive before other people.
He gave Himself to redeem sinners, forgive the guilty, reconcile the estranged, and make us His own.
And the Savior who calls us to follow Him also calls us to abide in Him.
In John 15:4, Jesus says:
“Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.” — KJV
The Greek verb is μείνατε (meinate), from μένω (menō), meaning to remain, stay, or abide.
Jesus is not describing an occasional religious performance.
He is describing continuing dependence upon Him.
A branch does not manufacture life by looking productive.
Its fruitfulness depends on remaining connected to the vine.
And this is where the question becomes impossible to ignore.
Are you remaining in Christ—or merely maintaining an image of someone who does?
Because those are not the same thing.
You can build an audience around Jesus without making your audience the measure of your faithfulness to Jesus.
You can receive hundreds of encouraging comments and still need to confess a sin nobody knows about.
You can have a beautifully organized collection of Bible verses and still struggle to obey the passage you read yesterday.
You can know how to sound spiritually mature while privately resisting the Lord's correction.
And yet, please hear this carefully.
The answer is not to abandon every public expression of faith.
The answer is to refuse to let public expression replace private devotion.
There is nothing wrong with sharing Scripture.
There is nothing wrong with Christian pages, ministries, videos, testimonies, or online discipleship.
There is nothing wrong with using technology to proclaim the Gospel.
The apostle Paul rejoiced when Christ was proclaimed, even while recognizing that some preached with deeply flawed motives (Philippians 1:15–18).
The message matters.
And so does the heart of the messenger.
But what happens when the messenger becomes more concerned about being seen as faithful than actually walking faithfully?
Jesus addressed the danger of religious performance directly.
In Matthew 6:5–6, He warned against praying in order to be seen by others. Then He instructed His disciples to pray privately to their Father.
The Greek word ταμεῖόν (tameion) in Matthew 6:6 refers to an inner room or private chamber.
The point was not that God can only be encountered in a particular physical room.
Nor was Jesus forbidding public prayer. Scripture itself contains faithful examples of believers praying together.
He was confronting the desire to use prayer as a performance for human approval.
The same principle reaches into our digital lives.
When you post a Bible verse, is your heart genuinely seeking to honor God?
When you share a testimony, are you grateful for His grace—or secretly dependent on people's reactions to feel spiritually significant?
When you write about holiness, are you also allowing Scripture to confront the hidden areas of your own life?
When you tell others to surrender, what are you still refusing to surrender?
Those questions are uncomfortable.
But they are worth asking.
Because sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not open rebellion.
It is becoming comfortable with religious appearances while resisting personal examination.
And there is a passage that should make every person who publicly speaks about Jesus approach that responsibility with humility.
In Matthew 7:22–23, Jesus warns that some will appeal to impressive religious works while lacking a genuine relationship with Him.
His words are sobering:
“And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23, KJV
This passage does not teach that an exhausted Christian who struggles to maintain a devotional routine has automatically lost salvation.
Nor does it mean that missing prayer on a difficult day proves someone never belonged to Christ.
Jesus is warning against false confidence in religious works apart from genuine allegiance to Him.
That distinction matters.
Because the purpose of this message is not to terrify a struggling believer into thinking salvation depends on perfect daily performance.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
But saving grace does not leave us indifferent to the Savior.
It teaches us to turn away from sin and grow in godliness (Titus 2:11–14).
And genuine faith is not content forever with an appearance of devotion that refuses the reality of obedience.
Perhaps that is why this message hurts.
Not because you don't love Jesus.
But because deep down, you know you have allowed other things to occupy the place your heart once reserved for Him.
You keep telling yourself you'll pray later.
After the work is finished.
After the children are asleep.
After the next video.
After one more message.
After one more scroll.
After life becomes less complicated.
But life keeps moving.
And later keeps becoming tomorrow.
Then tomorrow becomes another week.
And eventually you realize something heartbreaking.
You have spent more time watching other people talk about God than you have spent personally seeking Him.
You know what your favorite preacher said last Sunday.
You know which Christian post went viral.
You know which worship song everyone is sharing.
But you cannot remember the last time you opened the Bible without a notification interrupting you.
And suddenly the question is no longer about social media.
It is about your heart.
What have you been feeding it?
What have you been neglecting?
What have you allowed to become normal?
And what would change if you began giving Jesus the attention you so freely give to everything else?
Maybe the answer begins with a small, painfully honest prayer.
“Lord, I have been distracted.”
Not impressive.
Not eloquent.
Not something you need to post.
Just true.
“Lord, I've been telling others to trust You while struggling to bring my own fears before You.”
“Lord, I've been encouraging people to read their Bibles while neglecting Your Word myself.”
“Lord, I have become more concerned with looking like a strong Christian than admitting how desperately I need Your grace.”
“Lord, forgive me.”
And there, in that place of honesty, something beautiful can begin.
Not because your confession earns forgiveness.
But because the Gospel announces forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
The apostle John writes:
This promise is not permission to treat sin lightly.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and return to the truth.
The Christian life is not sustained by pretending we never drift, never struggle, and never need correction.
It is lived through continuing dependence upon the mercy and faithfulness of God.
And maybe someone reading this needs to hear something very specific.
Jesus is not asking you to manufacture a perfect devotional record before you come to Him.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting in His finished work rather than your religious achievements.
If you have wandered, don't turn your wandering into another excuse to stay away.
If your prayers have become rare, begin praying again.
If Scripture has remained unopened, open it.
If you have been hiding a sin beneath an impressive Christian image, bring it into the light and seek the help you need.
If you have become spiritually exhausted, remember that Christ's invitation is not reserved for people who have everything together.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
Jesus does not promise a life without hardship.
He calls the burdened to Himself.
And there is something profoundly comforting about the fact that the One who knows our hearts completely is also the One who welcomes repentant sinners.
Think about Peter.
He was outspoken.
Confident.
Ready to declare his loyalty to Jesus.
He insisted he would never deny Him.
Yet when the pressure came, Peter denied knowing the Lord three times.
Imagine the shame.
The memories.
The terrible contrast between what he had publicly promised and what he had privately done.
Peter knew what it meant for his words about Jesus to exceed the faithfulness of his actions.
But that was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter by the Sea of Tiberias.
In John 21, the risen Lord questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
The conversation was painful, personal, and restorative.
Peter's failure was not excused.
But neither was it allowed to be the final word over his life.
Grace met him there.
And the same Christ who restored Peter remains the hope of believers who have failed Him.
Not because our failures are harmless.
But because His mercy is greater than our ability to repair ourselves.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
From denial to restoration.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From spiritual pretense to honest surrender.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending our sin never happened.
Not by declaring repentance unnecessary.
Not by teaching that grace makes obedience optional.
But by saving sinners through His death and resurrection and transforming those who belong to Him.
Perhaps you will simply put your phone down.
Find a quiet place.
Open your Bible.
And say, “Jesus, I want to know You more deeply.”
No audience.
No camera.
No perfectly arranged coffee cup beside an open Bible.
No inspirational caption.
No need to prove anything to anyone.
Just you, coming before the Father through Jesus Christ.
Maybe you will read Psalm 51 and let David's confession teach you how to repent.
Maybe you will read John 15 and consider what it means to abide in Christ.
Maybe you will sit with Luke 10 and recognize yourself in Martha's distractions.
Maybe you will read Romans 8 and remember that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Maybe you will pray for five honest minutes.
Maybe longer.
The number of minutes is not the point.
This is not a competition to see who can spend the most time praying.
And private devotion is not a transaction in which we purchase God's love with our attention.
It is the response of a redeemed heart to the God who loved us first.
The goal is not to build another religious performance behind a closed door.
The goal is to know Christ, hear His Word, trust His promises, confess our sins, and follow Him in ordinary life.
Because a private prayer that nobody applauds can be an expression of genuine faith.
A quiet act of obedience that nobody sees can honor God.
An apology you finally offer.
A temptation you resist.
A person you forgive.
A burden you surrender.
A passage of Scripture you obey even when it costs you something.
These things may never go viral.
But they matter deeply.
And when the time comes to speak about Jesus publicly, your words can flow from a life increasingly shaped by His truth.
You don't have to stop posting about Jesus.
Just don't let posting about Him become a substitute for walking with Him.
Let the Bible verse you share be a verse you are willing to obey.
Let the prayer you post remind you to actually pray.
Let the testimony you tell remain rooted in gratitude rather than a hunger for attention.
Let your platform be a place of service, not a place where you measure your spiritual worth.
And remember that you do not need an audience to be loved by God.
You already have access to the Father through Christ.
That is a privilege no algorithm can give you and no decline in engagement can take away.
And if this article has exposed something in your heart, don't rush past it.
You do not need to write a long public confession or reveal private struggles to strangers.
But perhaps you can take one small, honest step.
And if God has been restoring your relationship with Him, consider sharing a testimony. Your words might encourage another believer who thinks they are the only one struggling.
Not every meaningful spiritual response needs to be public. Some things belong in prayer, trusted Christian fellowship, or pastoral care.
But a sincere word of encouragement can remind someone that they are not walking alone.
And perhaps there is someone in your family, a friend, a discouraged believer, a person drifting from the faith, or even someone who doesn't yet know Christ who needs to read this.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
Not because the Gospel needs an algorithm to remain powerful.
But because a simple act of sharing can place biblical encouragement in front of someone who might never have searched for it.
Because the aim of this ministry is not simply to gather an audience.
It is to point people to the Savior.
And that is also why I want to speak openly about something important.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people encounter biblical truth, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and find encouragement in their walk with Jesus.
Behind every article, devotional, teaching resource, and ministry effort is a desire to make the truth of Scripture accessible to more people.
These resources are part of our commitment to making Christian learning and spiritual encouragement available beyond the people who can afford to pay.
But producing, maintaining, and expanding a ministry requires time, resources, and faithful support.
And if Gospel Warrior has genuinely encouraged your walk with Christ, I want to invite you to become part of helping that work continue.
Some Christians may prayerfully choose to include support for a ministry like this within their regular charitable giving or offerings.
But let us be biblically clear.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing rather than pressured.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
In the Greek, ἱλαρὸν δότην (hilaron dotēn) means a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite support.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
And certainly not by claiming that financial support purchases His blessing.
Christ has already accomplished what no amount of money could ever accomplish for us.
Our salvation is His gift.
These products are not substitutes for Scripture or spiritual growth. They are simply additional resources and reminders that can accompany everyday Christian life.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, and grow.
You can still benefit from the free resources we make available.
And your encouragement, prayers, thoughtful comments, and willingness to share sound biblical teaching can also help this work reach others.
It is that you come to know Jesus Christ and continue growing in Him.
Because one day, every notification will fall silent.
The posts you spent hours perfecting will become yesterday's content.
The comments will stop arriving.
The numbers will lose their importance.
The platforms themselves may change beyond recognition.
But Jesus Christ remains the same.
And when you stand before Him, your confidence must not rest in how many people liked your Christian posts, how many articles you shared, or how publicly religious you appeared.
Your hope must rest in the crucified and risen Savior.
The One who bore sin.
The One who conquered death.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
The One who forgives, restores, and transforms.
So tonight, before you post another verse telling the world how wonderful Jesus is, perhaps spend a little time alone with Him.
Tell Him what you've been afraid to say.
Confess what you've been trying to hide.
Thank Him for mercy you could never deserve.
Read His Word without trying to turn every insight into content.
Pray for the people who need Him.
And ask Him to make your private life increasingly consistent with the faith you publicly proclaim.
Then, when you return to your screen, share the truth with a heart that remembers why it matters.
Not to impress people.
Not to prove you are holy.
Not to win an argument.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy to be known, loved, obeyed, and proclaimed.
And because someone on the other side of your screen may be longing for the very hope you have found in Him.
Don't become so busy telling the world that Jesus is worth knowing that you forget to spend your own life knowing Him.
